title: Ang 730–750: the Gurus in Suhi
hook: the one whose head He guards, on ang 749
tomorrow: which red fades in a week, and which one holds?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Suhi began: bright bronze that leaves black, and friends who walk with you all the way. Union. Today, a promise that's harder to hear than it sounds.

Helmets, car seats, a parent's hand on a kid's head in a crowd: people guard heads. On ang 749, Guru Arjan writes, in paraphrase: the one whose head you, Master, are over, how could that one suffer pain? It sounds like a promise that nothing will go wrong. A gentle note for anyone listening with kids: today mentions the Guru's own death, without detail.
screen: `A HAND ON A HEAD IN A CROWD.` → `HOW COULD THAT ONE SUFFER?` → `NOTHING WILL GO WRONG?`

segments.voice: These Suhi pages run through the Gurus in order, and ang 749 is Guru Arjan's. The hymn goes on, in paraphrase: you belong to the saints, and the saints are yours. Sikhs read 'guarded' in two ways. The first stays close to the letter: God protects. Its best case: Sikhs pray Ardas for protection, before a journey, an exam, a surgery, and the Granth tells of devotees like Prahlad kept safe. Why pray for protection if it isn't real? The second reading turns inward: the guarded head is a mind that can't be made to despair. Its best case is the writer himself. Sikhs remember that Guru Arjan was tortured and put to death, and tradition says he met it accepting God's will as sweet. If 'guarded' meant nothing bad happens, his own life would answer no. So this reading says the guard is over the head, not the body: the one who is held doesn't break. The two readings ask different things of the hymn. Both hear it as a real promise, and both say it in a dark room as well as a bright one. Guarded.
screen: `WHOSE HEAD YOU ARE OVER.` · `ONE READING: GOD PROTECTS.` · `ANOTHER: THE HELD MIND DOESN'T BREAK.` · `A PROMISE IN THE DARK ROOM TOO.` · then, large: `GUARDED.`

segments.voice: Sit tall and rest both hands on the crown of your head, elbows wide, for a few slow breaths. Then let your hands come down to your lap, and notice whether the head still feels held. Stay with that feeling for the sit.
Ang 730. Where the Gurus' hymns in Suhi run on, to Guru Arjan's on ang 749: whose head you are over, how could they suffer?
Guarded: the hand is over the head, in the bright room and the dark one. Held, fifteen thirty-six.
